title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to evaluate whether a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline yields higher validator pass rates than a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The confirmatory paired design used N=300 tasks (75 per intent cluster: reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The orchestration used a shared‑initial generation so baseline and guarded conditions began from the same candidate; the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one repair per failed candidate. Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair call); authoritative raw results file execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). Results: baseline 299/300 passes; guarded 300/300 passes; contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered target effect (0.10 absolute increase) was not observed due to a ceiling effect and minimal repair engagement (repair stage_count = 1). We provide artifact‑grounded analysis, concrete benchmark design recommendations, and complete disclosure and reproducibility pointers to the archived artifacts.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to assist NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, staged change planning, and automated remediation. Prior work documents the promise of LLMs and the recurrent risks of syntax, topology and semantic errors, hallucination, and prompt‑injection attacks; several prototype studies show improved final correctness when generation is coupled with deterministic verifiers and localized repair. However, the community lacks sealed, machine‑checkable benchmarks that pair intent tasks with explicit validator semantics and preregistered confirmatory tests of defended architectures. Motivated by that gap we preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 to answer a narrow confirmatory question under tightly constrained conditions: with a deterministic snapshot validator, a shared initial candidate per task, and a repair budget limited to one invocation per failed candidate, does a guarded GVR pipeline materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM? Our contributions are (1) a sealed, deterministic synthetic intent→configuration task bank and validator; (2) a preregistered paired experimental design and registered analysis executor; (3) a complete execution and analysis archive (preregistration SHA‑256 = a05938dad3a61e1f4aae518bcb42244009b0403a18387ceeff4be1d86ce87765; raw results SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...); and (4) an artifact‑grounded failure analysis and recommendations for future benchmark design.
sections.related_work: Surveys and recent focused studies document rapid growth in LLM applications for network management and identify verification, hallucination, and adversarial risks as central open problems [W4406137434, W4415071524, W4402742293]. Empirical prototypes show that LLMs can synthesize router and device configurations but often require verifier assistance or human adjudication to reach operational correctness [W4388629193; 10.1145/3626111.3628194]. Generate–validate–repair (GVR) and context‑aware prompting strategies have improved final correctness in focused proofs‑of‑concept [W4404652946], but those demonstrations are dataset‑ and method‑specific and typically limited in scale. Security analyses of prompt injection and adversarial prompts underscore practical threats to automated NetOps workflows and motivate guarded pipelines and hardened validators [W4405181600, W4388886073]. Our study situates itself as an archived, preregistered, machine‑checkable proof‑of‑concept benchmark that tests a narrowly defined operational claim under deterministic conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypothesis. We froze the experimental plan in preregistration ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 before execution. Primary confirmatory hypothesis H1: under a paired design with N=300 unique intent→topology tasks, a GVR pipeline (guarded) produces a higher per‑task binary validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator (baseline) (estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration documents task generation, validator semantics, exclusion rules, maximum_model_calls=600, maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1, and the analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 (exact McNemar; paired bootstrap CI; bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Its SHA‑256 is archived in the execution manifest.

Task bank construction. A deterministic task generator produced 300 synthetic tasks partitioned evenly across four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes: initial_state, expected_final_state, an intent textual description, allowed_fields, explicit workflow_policies, and a required_sequence (ordered field changes that the validator enforces). Tasks range in device counts 3–50 and abstract multi‑vendor models; all tasks are synthetic and redacted for private data. Representative task manifests and the full task_manifest.jsonl are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 062b80216e49a2919ebf8debd75cf02fffcfd752b5b253e5a11c0701ca853097).

Deterministic validator semantics. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implements the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator is a stateless snapshot checker: it (1) parses candidate commands into normalized actions, (2) enforces required_sequence order and workflow_policies (e.g., make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields), (3) computes the produced final_state, (4) compares final_state to expected_final_state, enumerates violation_codes and returns binary valid/invalid plus diagnostic traces (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count). The validator was intentionally conservative and deterministic to yield machine‑checkable binary outcomes suitable for confirmatory inference; per‑task scorer outputs are archived under execution/scoring/*.json.

Orchestration, shared generation, and repair budget. To isolate repair value we implemented a shared‑initial generation per task: a single shared candidate (shared_initial_generation) served as the baseline single‑pass output. The guarded condition validated that shared candidate and, only upon validator failure, was permitted up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This paired shared design ensures any guarded improvement originates from repair applied to the identical initial candidate rather than from sampling alternative initial candidates. Planned_episode_count = 600 (300 shared + up to 300 repair calls). The actual provider accounting recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}.

Model configuration and reproducible provider traces. The declared model was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version/requested_model = "gpt-5-mini") executed via the hosted adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with provider = "openai_responses". The execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) records: max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. In practice temperature = null combined with the hosted adapter's deterministic invocation semantics produced provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...). Because provider invoke‑time sampling semantics and model releases affect outputs, bit‑for‑bit reproduction requires either replaying the archived provider traces or access to the identical model release and invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json.

Analysis plan and pre-specified estimand. The primary estimand is the paired difference in per‑task binary validator pass rates (guarded minus baseline) computed on the N=300 paired outcomes. The preregistration specified the exact McNemar two‑sided test as the inferential routine and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed 1729). Sensitivity and missingness treatments were preregistered; the run completed with no missing or excluded pairs.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and provider audit. The execution manifest reports: started_at = 2026-08-29T12:41:43.384097+00:00; completed_at = 2026-08-29T13:07:38.995000+00:00; planned_episode_count = 600; completed_episode_count = 600; complete_pair_count = 300; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 301. Provider_call_audit (deterministic_reconciliation) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 301, cache_miss_count = 301, stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}, and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}. The authoritative raw results file is execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d); auditors can extract per‑call provider traces and the identifier of the single repair invocation from that file.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. Analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 55eacb88c64f29dc9c5ce1ca7079eca9b4a94b5d3a2970dae019a81a1decf73b; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55).

Repair engagement and discordant episode indexing. The guarded repair stage executed exactly once (stage_counts: repair = 1). The single repair provider call and the per‑episode discordant record (the sole baseline failure / the one discordant pair) are indexed inside execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). The execution manifest and raw results container function as the authoritative index: auditors wishing to identify the exact pair identifier (pair_id) and the standalone per‑call provider trace SHA‑256 should extract the single record in execution/raw_results.jsonl flagged with stage = "repair"; the raw_results artifact itself is archived under execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...). Representative per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json … task-000006-*.json) illustrate validator traces and difficulty labels; the single discordant episode is present in the full raw_results archive but not among the representative samples printed in this manuscript.

Interpretation and the ceiling effect. The exact McNemar test depends only on discordant counts n10 and n01; with n10 = 1 and n01 = 0 the test reports p = 1.0 under the pre‑specified two‑sided exact algorithm. Practically, this outcome reflects two facts visible in the archive: (A) near‑ceiling baseline performance (299/300) leaves very little headroom for a preregistered target effect of 0.10; (B) repair engagement was minimal (one repair invocation), so the guarded pipeline rarely differed from baseline. Arithmetic sensitivity: given the observed margins the maximum feasible paired difference is 0.00333, so the preregistered detectable effect (0.10 with ≈80% power at N=300 under conservative discordance assumptions) could not be realized on this task distribution. We therefore interpret the null confirmatory outcome as arising from an evaluative ceiling combined with an inert repair budget rather than an analytic error.
sections.discussion:
Scope and operational meaning of the null finding. The confirmatory null is specific to the sealed design: deterministic synthetic tasks, shared‑initial generation, a conservative snapshot validator, and a repair budget limited to one invocation per failed candidate. Under these conditions (high generator quality and strict repair trigger/budget), guarded repair provided minimal marginal benefit. This does not imply that GVR is generally unhelpful: in settings with lower generator reliability, adversarial inputs, stateful validators, or relaxed repair budgets, GVR is likely to produce measurable gains.

Concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations for future benchmark studies. The archived artifacts permit precise design choices to expose repair value: (1) raise initial failure rates by adding higher‑difficulty or adversarial seeds (the task manifest and per‑task difficulty labels in execution/task_manifest.jsonl quantify current difficulty distributions and show many tasks labeled medium/hard but still passed by the generator), (2) permit iterative repair budgets per failed candidate so repair can converge (stage_counts show repair=1 here), (3) evaluate multi‑generation baselines (sample k > 1 independent initial candidates per task) when selection value is of interest, (4) adopt stateful emulation validators that model ordered side effects and temporal constraints rather than only snapshot checks, and (5) include targeted prompt‑injection and adversarial test cases to assess guarded architectures under attack. Each recommendation maps directly to archived execution facts (300 shared generations vs 1 repair; per‑task validator traces) and can be implemented by altering preregistered sampling, repair policy, or validator semantics in future runs.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design controls generator variance but excludes evaluation of multi‑sample generator selection strategies. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot semantics and does not emulate vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, in‑flight temporal dynamics, or asynchronous side effects. External validity: tasks are synthetic and abstracted (device counts 3–50; abstract vendor models) and only one declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one validator version (v5.0) were evaluated; generalization to production networks or other models is unproven. Conclusion validity: with only one discordant outcome exploratory subgroup or failure‑mode clustering is underpowered. These threats are documented in the archived manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifact (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a preregistered paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Results show near‑perfect pass rates for both approaches (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR yields a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported under the sealed design; the null is attributable to a ceiling effect and minimal repair engagement (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1; raw results SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...). We release the full preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable the community to extend the benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, and multi‑model comparisons to evaluate when GVR pipelines provide operational value. All archived artifacts referenced in this paper are authoritative and indexed by the execution manifest for deterministic verification and reuse.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in execution/model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 0d841d29...).

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and execution/raw_results.jsonl) and are authoritative for auditors.
